Process

How I work

I open the problem up, then narrow it down, twice.

  1. Open up

    Empathise

    Immersion, interviews and interactions, netnography, secondary research and expert opinions.

  2. Narrow down

    Define

    Affinity mapping, fishbone diagram, jobs to be done and a how-might-we question.

  3. Open up

    Ideate

    Mind mapping, Crazy 8, storyboards and rapid prototypes.

  4. Narrow down

    Prototype and test

    A prototype tested with users, then revised from what they said.

Research case study · 2025

Addressing the gaps in higher education among tribal youth

A field research capstone for IIT Delhi Design Thinking and Innovation. I started with an open theme, education in tribal communities, and no defined problem. The problem emerged after immersion.

Context
Field research capstone, IIT Delhi Design Thinking and Innovation
Where
Vazhachal, Thrissur (Kadar community) and two Paniya colonies in Wayanad
Methods
Immersion, in-depth interviews, netnography, expert input, secondary research
Output
AadiYouth, a voice-assisted guidance app prototype

Problem

Young people leave school without a next step

In the Vazhachal hamlet and the Paniya colonies, many students stop after higher secondary and go into daily wage work. They do not know which college to choose, or when and where to apply.

I built a persona from the field research to keep that experience in view while I worked.

How might we help Jaya and her friends engage in higher studies, considering their cultural aspects?

Persona

Jaya

20 · Daily wage worker · Vazhachal, Kerala

Jaya finished higher secondary a year ago at the school nearest her hamlet. Her parents are daily wage workers. She dropped her studies because she did not know what to do next.

Goals

  • Go to her daily wage work
  • Look after her family

Challenge

  • She struggles to speak and write when she goes to hospitals and government offices.
ThinksShe needs a system that can guide youth like her.
DoesGoes to daily wage work and cares for her parents.
Says“I don’t know who I should approach or what steps I should take to learn.”
FeelsFrustrated when she goes outside. Sad that she dropped her studies.

Research

How I researched it

  1. ImmerseVisited the Vazhachal hamlet, two Paniya colonies and a Jesuit-run tribal organisation. Kept a field journal at every site.
  2. ListenFour in-depth interviews with a tribal chieftain, an activist, a scholar and a writer.
  3. Cross-checkNetnography, conversations with NGOs and tribal department officials, and census and state data.
  4. SynthesiseFour personas, three empathy maps, affinity mapping from eight themes to three, a fishbone diagram and five whys.

Getting access

Entry to the hamlets is restricted. A forest officer questioned my purpose for about 45 minutes before I could go in. Officials told me about past harm from outside researchers, so I explained my purpose plainly and followed their procedures. A teacher in Wayanad helped me visit the two Paniya colonies.

Staying flexible

Interviews with the chieftain and an activist were postponed three times because of wildlife incidents. I stayed in touch, rescheduled around them and used the waiting time for site visits and secondary research.

Findings

What the field showed

  • Language barrierChildren speak a tribal language. Some tenth graders still need a scribe in exams.
  • Cultural gapSchool culture and methods are unfamiliar to tribal children.
  • DiscriminationStudents face discrimination from peers and teachers.
  • Low awareness at homeLittle awareness in families of why education matters.
  • Financial pressureDaily wage responsibilities, and grants and scholarships that arrive inconsistently.
  • Lack of guidanceStudents do not know where, or whom, to approach for help with college.

I narrowed these to three priorities: guidance, dropouts and language.

Solution

AadiYouth

I explored ideas with mind mapping and Crazy 8, then chose the most feasible one by user context, time and budget. The result was a minimum viable product: a mobile app for people like Jaya.

  • Community groups
  • Internet facility to self-learn
  • Guidance from educated people
  • E-service centres
  • WhatsApp groups
  • Guidance programs
  • Co-learning spaces
  • Mobile application
  • GuidanceCarefully curated material from experts.
  • LearningLanguage learning from educated tribal people.
  • EncouragementEncourage tribal youth to take up higher studies.

Impact

What testing changed

Five tribal youth tried the prototype. They found it simple and quick to move through, and asked for more readable text. Tribal children also find the written language hard to read, so I added a voice command to every option.

AaText size 28
→
AaText size 40
  • Typeface changed to Roboto, a more readable face
  • Text size raised from 28 to 40
  • A voice command added to every option

This was early validation with a prototype and no launch, so there are no usage figures yet.

Limits

What I would do next

The study covered two communities, four interviews and five testers, so the findings point in a direction and are not conclusive. The next step is to validate them with more tribal communities and test a working version with more users.

Design case study · Mobile app

Insight for Innovation: a mobile app for an education NGO

Insight For Innovation (IFI) is an NGO that empowers school children by helping them learn with the help of college students. The IFI mobile app manages and coordinates the tasks in its education projects.

Client
Insight For Innovation, an education NGO
Product
Mobile app for managing and coordinating education project tasks
My role
UX research and UI/UX design
Deliverables
Research, wireframes, Figma prototype, design system, hi-fi screens

Problem and goal

Scattered work, no clear overview

The problem

Organizations struggled with fragmented innovation processes. Ideas were lost in emails, spreadsheets lacked visibility, and there was no structured way to evaluate or prioritize concepts. Teams needed a centralized, intuitive platform.

The goal

Design a mobile-first experience that empowers teams to submit ideas effortlessly, collaborate in real time, and track innovation pipelines with clear metrics, ultimately fostering a culture of continuous improvement.

Process

Four stages, from research to build

  1. 01 DiscoverStakeholder interviews, a competitive analysis and user surveys to find the key pain points in existing workflows.
    • 12 stakeholder interviews
    • Survey with 150+ respondents
    • Competitive audit of 8 platforms
    • 3 user personas
  2. 02 Define and ideateResearch findings turned into insights, journey maps and ideation workshops that produced design concepts.
    • Affinity mapping sessions
    • How Might We brainstorming
    • User journey and empathy maps
    • Feature prioritization matrix
  3. 03 Wireframe and prototypeLow-fidelity wireframes for quick validation, then an interactive prototype for usability testing with target users.
    • 20+ wireframe screens
    • Interactive Figma prototype
    • 3 rounds of usability testing
    • Task success rate benchmarking
  4. 04 Visual designA visual design system with consistent type, colour and components, then discussions with developers.
    • Design system with 60+ components
    • Hi-fi designs with 40+ screens

Solution

Hi-fi screens

Sign-up, a student list, test conduction and evaluation, a rewards system for volunteers, and a school mapping flow.

Impact

What changed after launch

  • 40%increase in task completion rate
  • 92%user satisfaction score (SUS)
  • 60%fewer support tickets post-launch

Key learnings

What I took from it

  • Early user involvement pays offTesting wireframes with real users before high-fidelity design caught navigation issues that would have been expensive to fix later.
  • Design systems accelerate iterationA reusable component library from day one let the team explore more layout variations in less time.
